script.title: Why McCoy Made Steam Engines Oil Themselves

lines: A certified engineer went to work oiling railroad engines.
Elijah McCoy was born free in Ontario in 1844.
His parents had escaped slavery in Kentucky.
At 15, McCoy was sent to Scotland.
He studied in Edinburgh and became a certified mechanical engineer.
But when McCoy arrived in Michigan, he could find work only as a fireman and oiler.
Trains needed to stop for lubrication and maintenance.
In a home-based machine shop in Ypsilanti, McCoy also worked on inventions.
In 1872, he patented an automatic lubricator for steam engines.
It was for oiling the engines of locomotives and ships.
You see, it's like a self-watering plant pot.
Nobody has to stop and pour.
Lubricators let trains run faster, with less need to stop.
By 1899, the McCoy lubricator was in use on almost all North American railroads.
But McCoy lacked the money to make his lubricators in large numbers.
So he usually sold his patent rights to investors, or assigned them to his employers.
He obtained as many as 57 patents, even a lawn sprinkler.
A popular story says engineers asked for his oiler by name: the real McCoy.
That story is false.
The phrase actually comes from Scotland, and has nothing to do with Elijah McCoy.

claims.claim: Elijah McCoy was born free in 1844 in Colchester, Ontario, to parents who had escaped slavery in Kentucky.
At the age of 15, in 1859, Elijah McCoy was sent to Scotland; after studying at the University of Edinburgh, he was certified as a mechanical engineer.
When Elijah McCoy arrived in Michigan, he could find work only as a fireman and oiler at the Michigan Central Railroad.
In a home-based machine shop in Ypsilanti, McCoy did more highly skilled work, such as developing improvements and inventions.
He invented an automatic lubricator for oiling the steam engines of locomotives and ships, patenting it in 1872 (U.S. patent 129,843).
Lubricators enabled trains to run faster and more profitably with less need to stop for lubrication and maintenance.
By 1899, the Michigan Bureau of Labor and Industrial Statistics reported that the McCoy lubricator was in use on almost all North American railroads.
Lacking the capital with which to manufacture his lubricators in large numbers, he usually assigned his patent rights to his employers or sold them to investors.
He continued to invent until late in life, obtaining as many as 57 patents, including a folding ironing board and a lawn sprinkler.
A false etymology claims railroad engineers would request his invention by name, the real McCoy; the phrase actually originates from Scotland and has nothing to do with Elijah McCoy.

cast.mccoy: a 28 year old Black Canadian-American engineer, tall and lean, a narrow dark brown face, a neat short black moustache, short black hair, wearing a soot-smudged indigo blue work shirt, brown leather braces and a grey cloth cap, 1870s
cast.mother: a 30 year old Black woman, slim, a warm oval face with high cheekbones, black hair wrapped in a mustard yellow headscarf, wearing a rust red wool dress with a cream shawl, 1840s
cast.teen: a 15 year old Black boy, thin, a round boyish face with bright brown eyes, close-cropped black hair, wearing a slightly big brown tweed jacket over a white shirt and a dark green neckerchief, 1850s
cast.investor: a 55 year old American businessman, heavy build, a pink jowly face, white mutton-chop sideburns, a black silk top hat, wearing a dark grey frock coat over a burgundy waistcoat, 1870s
cast.older: a 60 year old Black engineer, a lined dark brown face, short grey hair, a full grey moustache, small round spectacles, wearing a charcoal wool suit with a white shirt and a black bow tie, 1900s
